slides.headline: 3 ADHD Myths That Are Straight-Up Wrong
slides.sub: You've probably heard at least one of these. Maybe someone said it to your face. Let's burn them down.
slides.kicker: spoiler: it was never just boys

slides.headline: ADHD is something kids grow out of eventually
ADHD follows most people into adulthood
slides.body: About 60-70% of children with ADHD continue to meet diagnostic criteria as adults. The hyperactivity often goes quiet — turning inward as racing thoughts, restlessness, and an inability to wind down — which is exactly why so many adults get missed entirely. The brain differences don't disappear; the mask just gets more practiced.

slides.headline: Girls and women would be diagnosed if they really had it
Women are diagnosed an average 4 years later
slides.body: Girls are socialized to internalize struggles rather than externalize them, so instead of climbing walls they ruminate, people-please, and exhaust themselves compensating. A 2020 study in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry found clinicians rated identical ADHD symptoms as less severe when the child was described as a girl. The disorder is the same. The detection is not.

slides.headline: If you can hyperfocus, you can't have ADHD
ADHD is a regulation problem, not an attention shortage
slides.body: The ADHD brain doesn't lack attention — it lacks consistent, voluntary control over where attention goes. Hyperfocus happens when the brain latches onto a high-dopamine task and basically can't let go, which is the same dysregulation in a different direction. You can lose four hours to a single Wikipedia thread and still be completely unable to start a ten-minute work email.

slides.headline: You're not lazy. You're not making it up.
slides.body: These myths delay diagnosis by years and leave a lot of people — especially women and adults — quietly blaming themselves for something neurological. Knowing the truth is the first step to actually getting support.
slides.commentPrompt: Which of these myths have you personally been told? Drop it in the comments 👇

caption:
The report card said 'smart but doesn't apply herself.' The therapist said 'you're too articulate to have ADHD.' The doctor said 'aren't you a bit old for this?'

None of that was true. All of it was harmful.

ADHD isn't a childhood phase, it isn't just a 'boy thing,' and the ability to hyperfocus doesn't cancel out a diagnosis — it's actually part of the same pattern.

These three myths are some of the most common reasons people spend years — sometimes decades — undiagnosed and unsupported.

Which one have you heard most in your own life? Tell me in the comments.

slides.headline: which adhd morning are you having?
slides.sub: four types. one is painfully you. comment your letter.

slides.body: You set six alarms. You turned off five of them with zero memory of doing it. The sixth one you snoozed until it became a different problem entirely. You finally got up forty minutes late, stood in the shower fully clothed for a second, and now you're apologizing to your boss again.

You woke up on time. You genuinely did. But you picked up your phone 'just to check the time' and now it's been 47 minutes and you've watched three videos about a topic you didn't care about yesterday. Getting up now feels impossible and you're not even sure why.

You overslept, skipped breakfast, couldn't find the left shoe for nine full minutes, and left the house with wet hair and a granola bar in your mouth. You were somehow only four minutes late. Your nervous system thinks this is a normal Tuesday. It is a normal Tuesday.

You didn't oversleep. You never went to sleep. At 2am your brain decided it was absolutely the moment to reorganize your entire file system or research the history of a country you'll never visit. It's now 6am, you feel oddly productive, and you will crash completely by noon.

slides.headline: whichever letter you picked
slides.body: All four of these are attention-regulation patterns — the ADHD brain struggling to initiate, transition, or modulate arousal at the start of the day. None of them mean you're lazy, unmotivated, or 'bad at adulting.' They mean your brain's alarm system runs on a different operating system, and shame is not a software update that fixes it.

slides.headline: Set up tomorrow tonight in 10 minutes
slides.sub: Morning ADHD chaos usually starts the night before — scattered stuff, no plan, zero runway. This reset builds tomorrow's structure so your future self doesn't have to improvise at 7am with no coffee.

slides.headline: Do a 2-minute brain dump
slides.body:
Grab any paper or open a notes app and write everything rattling around in your head — tasks, worries, random things you remembered. Don't organize it, don't judge it. Just get it out.

Why it works: your working memory is not a storage system, it's RAM — and it's been running too many tabs all day. Externalizing thoughts onto paper frees up cognitive load so your brain can actually rest tonight.

Example: 'email Dr. Singh, pack lunch, find Maya's permission slip, that weird thing I said in 2019' — all of it goes on the page.

slides.headline: Pick your ONE anchor task
slides.body:
Look at your brain dump and circle the single most important thing you need to do tomorrow — not the most urgent, the most important. Write it at the top of a fresh sticky note or tomorrow's calendar slot.

Why it works: ADHD brains struggle with task prioritization under activation pressure (i.e., when you're already stressed at 8am). Deciding NOW, when your nervous system is calmer, removes that real-time decision cost entirely.

Example: instead of 'finish the whole report,' your anchor is 'write the intro paragraph before lunch.'

slides.headline: Set out three physical items
slides.body:
Choose three things you'll need tomorrow and put them somewhere you cannot miss them — by the door, on your bag, literally on your shoes. Physical objects in physical space beat mental reminders every time.

Why it works: ADHD makes object permanence genuinely harder — out of sight is functionally out of mind. Visible cues bypass the need to remember and lower activation energy because half the prep work is already done.

Example: headphones, the library book that's two weeks overdue, and your water bottle — all sitting on top of your bag right now.
slides.kicker: if you can see it, done

slides.headline: Write tomorrow's start time down
slides.body:
Pick a specific time you'll begin your anchor task — not 'morning,' not 'when I'm ready,' but an actual clock time. Write it where you'll see it first thing, like your phone lock screen or a sticky note on the coffee maker.

Why it works: vague intentions don't activate the ADHD brain — specificity does. A defined time creates an implementation intention, which research shows significantly increases follow-through, especially when initiation is your biggest barrier.

Example: 'I will start the intro paragraph at 9:15am, at my desk, with my phone in the other room.'

slides.headline: Create a tiny morning gift
slides.body:
Do one small thing right now that will genuinely help tomorrow-you — prep the coffee, charge your devices, put your meds next to your toothbrush, set a kind alarm label. Make it feel like leaving a note for a friend.

Why it works: dopamine responds to novelty and reward anticipation — framing this as caring for a future person (even if that person is you) makes it feel meaningful enough to actually do. Removing friction the night before dramatically lowers morning activation energy.

Example: pre-making a playlist called 'work brain on' and setting it to open automatically when your alarm goes off.

slides.headline: your toolkit
You don't have to overhaul your life tonight.
slides.body: start with one. literally just one.
slides.commentPrompt: Which step are you trying tonight? Drop it below — we'll cheer you on 👇

caption:
Your ADHD mornings might be chaotic because your evenings have no structure — and that's not a character flaw, it's a setup problem.

This 10-minute evening reset isn't about discipline or willpower. It's about working WITH your brain's wiring: externalizing your working memory, reducing morning activation energy, and giving your future self a fighting chance before the day even starts.

The whole thing takes less time than doom-scrolling before bed, and it actually changes how tomorrow feels.

slides.headline: The ADHD struggles nobody has a name for
Waiting Mode
slides.body:
When you have one thing coming up, your brain locks the whole day until it's done. You can't start anything else because the event owns you.

You have a 3pm call so you do nothing from 9am onward.
You sit near the door 40 minutes early because leaving felt impossible to time.
You cancel morning plans rather than risk 'losing track' before the appointment.

slides.headline: Decision Paralysis
slides.body:
It's not indecisiveness. Your brain generates every possible option simultaneously and can't rank them, so it freezes entirely.

You spend 25 minutes choosing where to order lunch and then just don't eat.
You open four browser tabs for the same product and close them all without buying.
You stand in the shower deciding which task to do first until the water goes cold.

slides.headline: Auditory Processing Lag
slides.body:
You heard the words. Your brain just needed an extra three seconds to assemble them into meaning — and by then everyone moved on.

Someone gives you verbal directions and you nod, then realize you retained nothing.
You ask 'wait, what?' not because you weren't listening but because it landed late.
On calls you answer the question before last because your processing is one beat behind.

slides.headline: The Wall of Awful
slides.body:
Tasks don't feel hard because they're difficult. They feel hard because your brain has layered every past failure, criticism, and embarrassment onto them.

You cannot open the email because the last time you did something similar you got it wrong.
The dishes aren't about dishes — they're about every time someone said you were lazy.
You postpone the form for three weeks and hate yourself daily, which makes it harder to start.

slides.headline: Hyperfixation Crash
slides.body:
After hours of hyperfocus, the interest switch flips off without warning and you can't access the motivation again no matter how hard you try.

You learn an entire new skill in a weekend then can't open the app again for six months.
You're mid-project, genuinely excited, and wake up the next morning completely unable to care.
People call it giving up. You call it the engine just stopped and you don't have the key.

slides.headline: You're not broken.
slides.body: Every trait here was explained to you as a character flaw. It wasn't. It isn't.
slides.commentPrompt: Which one hit hardest? Drop the number below — 1 through 5.

caption:
Your ADHD isn't laziness, flakiness, or a bad attitude. It's a brain that processes time, decisions, emotions, and sound differently — and nobody handed you the manual.

Waiting Mode isn't poor planning. The Wall of Awful isn't avoidance for no reason. The auditory processing lag is why you nodded and then had no idea what was just said.

These patterns have names. And naming them is where it starts to get easier.

slides.headline: dear diary: i just wanted to go to sleep

slides.body: Okay. Bedtime. I am doing this. I put my phone across the room, got into bed, and immediately remembered I never replied to that text from three weeks ago. It's urgent now, for some reason. At 10:47pm.
I got up to get water. I am now reorganizing the tupperware cabinet. I don't know how I got here. The water is on the counter, untouched.
Back in bed. Started a completely new sleep playlist. Spent 22 minutes on the playlist. Did not close my eyes once. The playlist is genuinely excellent, though.
Brain has launched a full investigation into something embarrassing I said in 2009. Evidence is being reviewed. A verdict is expected never. I have to be up in six hours.

I have now googled: 'why can't I fall asleep,' 'do I have anxiety OR is it ADHD,' 'both?', and 'what is the best mattress.' I have added two mattresses to a cart I will never check out. I am so tired.

slides.headline: it was never laziness
slides.body:
The ADHD brain struggles to downshift — not because you won't stop, but because the brakes don't work the same way. Executive function controls more than tasks. It controls transitions, including the one from awake to asleep.

You're not broken. You're running on a nervous system that genuinely has a harder time letting go. That's real, it's documented, and it's not your fault.

dear diary: I just wanted a normal bedtime. it did not go well.

The tupperware cabinet is now organized by size. The 2009 memory has been fully relitigated. Two mattresses are sitting in a cart somewhere. And sleep? Sleep is still pending.

ADHD doesn't clock out at bedtime — the same executive function that makes it hard to start tasks also makes it hard to stop them. The transition to sleep is a transition, and transitions are genuinely hard for our brains.

slides.headline: there's a word for that thing you do
slides.sub: it's the stack of mail, clothes, forms, and feelings you keep meaning to get to — and somehow never do

defs: a physical accumulation of items an ADHD brain has flagged as requiring effortful decision-making, causing repeated avoidance until the pile becomes so large it feels emotionally insurmountable
the leaning tower of 'I'll deal with this later' that has been silently judging you from the corner for six weeks
slides.example: "The doom pile started with one jury duty notice and somehow absorbed a birthday card, three chargers, a library book from 2022, and my entire sense of self-worth."

slides.headline: the corner that runs the house
slides.body: There's a corner in the living room you've stopped looking at directly. It started with one piece of mail that needed 'just a quick phone call' to sort out. Your brain filed it under 'high stakes, do later' — and later never came, so everything else that felt hard landed on top of it.

slides.headline: the office chair method
slides.body: It's not just surfaces. For a lot of ADHD brains, the doom pile is also the chair — the one in the bedroom buried under clothes that aren't dirty enough for the hamper but aren't clean enough to hang up. Every item there required a small judgment call your executive function didn't have bandwidth for. So it landed on the chair. The chair understands.

slides.headline: the form that cost you everything
slides.body: The school sent home a permission slip in September. It needed a signature, a check for $12, and to be returned by Friday. Each of those steps felt like a separate task to an ADHD brain running on empty. By October it was somewhere in the doom pile, and you got the email asking if your kid was coming on the trip. You knew where the form was. You just couldn't get to it. That's not carelessness. That's a working memory and initiation problem with a paper trail.

slides.headline: naming it changes it
slides.body: When something is nameless, it feels like a character flaw — 'I'm just messy, I'm just lazy, I'm just a disaster.' When it has a name, it becomes a pattern with a cause. Doom pile tells you something specific: these items stalled because they each required initiation, decision-making, or emotional energy your brain wasn't allocating. That's not a moral failure — that's neuroanatomy. And patterns with causes have workarounds.

slides.headline: now you have the word
slides.body: use it. share it. save it for the next time someone says 'just deal with it when it arrives'.
slides.commentPrompt: What word would YOU add to the ADHD dictionary? Drop it in the comments — we might feature it next Saturday.

caption:
There's a clinical reason your mail pile has its own gravitational pull — and it has a name.

The doom pile isn't clutter. It's a symptom. Every item in it got flagged by your brain as "requires effort I don't have right now" — and because ADHD brains struggle with task initiation and working memory, "right now" never arrived. The pile grew. The shame grew louder than the pile.

Naming it doesn't magic it away, but it does stop you from reading it as proof that you're broken. You're not broken. You have a brain that taxes certain tasks differently.

slides.headline: Sunday is not a productivity deadline
slides.sub: You don't owe the week a better version of yourself by Monday.

slides.headline: Rest is not something you earn
slides.body: You needed it before you accomplished anything today.

slides.headline: The undone list can wait one day
slides.body: It survived Saturday. It will survive Sunday too.

slides.headline: Recharging counts as doing something
slides.body: Your nervous system is not being lazy. It is working.

slides.headline: You are not behind on being okay
slides.body: There is no schedule for feeling like yourself again.

slides.headline: Your permission slip for this week
slides.body: You are allowed to skip the Sunday reset routine entirely.

slides.headline: see you monday
slides.body: same brain. no new you required.
slides.commentPrompt: Tell us one thing you are NOT doing today. Drop it below — no guilt allowed.

caption:
Sunday is not a productivity deadline.

Somewhere along the way, Sunday became a second chance to fix everything — meal prep, inbox zero, a full week planned out by 8pm. For ADHD brains that already run on fumes by Friday, that pressure doesn't reset anything. It just adds one more thing you didn't do right.

You don't have to optimize today. You don't have to feel ready. You just have to exist in it for a little while.
